body.text: Organised crime networks, often based abroad, are using social media not to spread an ideology but to turn followers into couriers, lookouts, and weapon traders

The use of social media by terror groups for propaganda, ideological messaging, and information warfare is, by now, a well-established threat. Indian security agencies actively monitor it, and official policy documents, such as the Ministry of Home Affairs’ PRAHAAR counter-terrorism strategy, explicitly name it as an ongoing concern, warning that radical groups continue to try to recruit Indian youth online. What is less discussed, and arguably harder to counter, is a parallel shift: organised crime networks, often based outside India, are using the same platforms not chiefly to spread an ideology but to build a brigade of foot soldiers who work as drug couriers, lookouts, and, sometimes, weapon traders.

The case of Shahzad Bhatti, the Pakistan- and UAE-based social media personality accused by Indian agencies of running a crime-terror network backed by Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), illustrates this shift. Such networks have turned publicity into a weapon: attacks are filmed, claimed, and circulated within hours, serving two purposes at once — frightening the public and advertising the gang’s reach to its next recruits. Bhatti is one figure in a wider pattern that police from Delhi to Rajasthan now describe as a settled recruitment model rather than a one-off case.

Investigators describe Bhatti’s network as a graded system. Handlers track who engages with their content, make direct contact, and start recruits on low-risk, low-paid tasks that pay between INR 5,000-10,000, such as dropping a package at a specified location or passing on information about police checkposts. Recruits who prove reliable are moved on to the network’s actual business lines: carrying narcotics and weapons trafficked from Pakistan through Punjab into Delhi-NCR; photographing and filming railway stations, cantonments, and other installations; and, closer to the border, installing CCTV units and gathering footage, as well as recording GPS coordinates of police posts and other security infrastructure. In one case, in June 2026, authorities arrested a 20-year-old in Rajasthan’s Hanumangarh district for filming local police stations, complete with exact coordinates, and forwarding the material to an account identifying itself as Bhatti’s.

Indian sociologists and police officials often point to the lure of quick money, power, and respect as key drivers, all of which appear to be at work in Bhatti’s case. Punjab, in particular, has a well-documented culture in which gangster life is openly glamorised, with music videos celebrating guns and “gangland” status routinely drawing tens of millions of views. A 22-year-old Ludhiana resident told ThePrint that he had grown up on songs glamorising power, guns, and displays of wealth, and that young people like him are drawn to that lifestyle. For youth with few job prospects and little to look forward to, that pull is hard to resist, and it is precisely this vulnerability that such networks are built to find and exploit.
What sets this apart from earlier generations of criminal recruitment is how little friction it involves. No face-to-face meeting is needed; all it takes is a public account and a direct message.

What sets this apart from earlier generations of criminal recruitment is how little friction it involves. No face-to-face meeting is needed; all it takes is a public account and a direct message. Bhatti’s recruiters reportedly worked from the inside out, identifying potential recruits within the existing audience of his social media account and gradually expanding the network. The handlers monitored who liked or commented on his posts and approached the most engaged followers first. Some followers, meanwhile, messaged entirely on their own initiative, sharing photographs of weapons.

Bhatti is part of a wider ecosystem of gang leaders who have made open, camera-ready defiance of Indian security forces part of their brand. Lawrence Bishnoi runs much of his operation from behind bars, allegedly directing, by phone, a network estimated to number in the hundreds. He has also sought to cultivate the image of a patriot in the mould of Bhagat Singh, wearing T-shirts printed with the revolutionary’s face, a practice that prison officials suspect is deliberate image-building. His gang, meanwhile, has used social media to taunt security agencies directly, including by posting an open threat online.

His Canada-based associate, Satwinder Singh, alias Goldy Brar, has gone further still, turning claims of responsibility into a real-time media strategy. Brar publicly claimed the 2022 murder of singer-politician Sidhu Moose Wala on Facebook within hours, and has since claimed several other killings.

Taken together with Bhatti’s case, these examples show a common pattern: leaders who are easily accessible to their followers through direct messages on a social media account, even though they sit far away. Another shared feature is that these gangsters outsource the operational work, such as killings, extortion, smuggling, and recruitment, to others. Many recruits never meet their handlers in person, which is one reason courts find it so hard to extradite gangsters.

Enforcement alone cannot keep pace with this recruitment model, because arresting one courier does not remove the demand for the next. affected youth with few job prospects and little to look forward to are precisely the people these networks are built to find, which means the most durable fix looks less like policing and more like economic and social investment. Skilling programmes, local employment, and legitimate outlets for young men’s competitive energy and desire for status are all needed. Police repeatedly cite sport, in particular, as an alternative to gang life for the same demographic these networks target.

State-level de-radicalisation models, such as family- and community-based referral systems, are better suited to small towns, because they rely on people who already know when a young person is spending unusual amounts of time online or has suddenly come into unexplained money. Extending that model beyond the handful of states that currently run it, and funding it at the panchayat and district levels rather than only through state police headquarters, is essential.

Banks can also serve as an early warning system, as recruits are typically paid through small, sub-threshold transfers. If banks flagged patterns of small, regular transactions in an account, they could interrupt a recruitment long before the recruit is sent on a courier run. The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal and its 24/7 helpline, 1930, already exist as a channel for the public to flag suspicious online contact of this kind. They are oriented chiefly towards financial fraud, however, and extending them to cover gang and terror recruitment attempts explicitly would close an obvious gap.

The other half of the answer lies with the social media platforms. India’s Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code Rules require platforms to acknowledge and act on takedown requests within three hours, and the Home Ministry’s Sahyog portal now lets police officers issue bulk takedown requests directly to intermediaries. Bhatti’s own accounts, which have been repeatedly barred and just as repeatedly recreated under new names ending in “333”, illustrate both sides of the problem: platforms do act once an account is flagged, but reactive, complaint-driven takedown does little against an account that can reappear under a new name within days.

The Bhatti case points to three areas where action is needed. First, platforms should use proactive pattern detection to identify clusters of repeat-offender accounts, rather than waiting for each new “333” account to be reported individually. Second, platforms should publish disaggregated data on organised-crime and terror-recruitment takedowns in India, separate from broader, consolidated takedown figures. Third, legal cooperation between Indian authorities, social media platforms, and foreign governments should be made faster and more effective, since a domestic takedown regime, however fast, cannot fully address the problem on its own.
